html:
SMTO-EXE-0221 — The Gateway isn't allowed to use Docker on that computer

GUID: 21b5568a-70cd-5c07-a7e6-37c4837c73ea
Slug: docker-permission-denied
Domain: EXE · Subsystem: docker

What happened

  • The Gateway, SMTO's helper program on that computer, tried to use Docker, but the computer refused because the Gateway's user account doesn't have permission. This request didn't change anything.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Find out which user account the Gateway runs as on that computer. This is the account that installed and starts the Gateway, not your SMTO sign-in. Docker checks the account the Gateway runs as when deciding whether to allow it.
  2. Ask that computer's administrator to let that account use Docker (on Linux, usually by adding it to the docker group), then restart the Gateway program. New Docker access only takes effect after the Gateway starts again.
  3. Don't run the Gateway as an administrator or root account just to fix this. Full control of the computer is far more access than Docker needs.
  4. Ask SMTO to repeat the Docker request. Nothing changed the first time, so it's safe to repeat once access is fixed.

What success looks like

  • SMTO can list the Docker containers on that Gateway without a permission message.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to that computer's administrator. If Docker there uses its own access rules, they need to allow this account too.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The Gateway's local Docker Engine request was refused: opening the socket raised PermissionError, or the Engine returned 401/403 on a non-image endpoint.

What this means

  • Access to the local Engine socket raised PermissionError, or the Engine returned a non-registry authentication/authorization status. Docker execution remains on the selected Gateway and its explicitly configured local Engine. Preserve accepted private references, exact object identities, completed prefixes and unknown effects; diagnostics never replay a mutation.

Why this can happen

  • Access to the local Engine socket raised PermissionError, or the Engine returned a non-registry authentication/authorization status.

How to diagnose it

  • Distinguish OS socket access from an Engine rejection using the retained phase/status; do not assume all denials require a socket ownership change.

How to fix it

  • As the Gateway's service account, run docker version against the endpoint in GATEWAY_DOCKER_ENDPOINT and fix socket access (for example docker group membership, or the correct rootless socket path) or the Engine authorization rule that denied the call, then restart the Gateway. Do not run the Gateway as root or widen unrelated host permissions.
  • Correct the established socket or Engine authorization prerequisite without broadening unrelated host permissions.

Retry and execution caution

  • Verify the selected Gateway account can access its explicitly configured local Docker socket.

How to verify the fix

  • The exact intended Engine request is permitted under deliberately configured account access.

What not to do

  • Never automatically replay an uncertain Docker mutation.

Technical notes

  • Docker execution remains on the selected Gateway and its explicitly configured local Engine. Preserve accepted private references, exact object identities, completed prefixes and unknown effects; diagnostics never replay a mutation.
